question: Tell me about a time you resolved a disagreement between colleagues or team members.

raiseTranscript.text: Tell me about a time you resolved a disagreement between colleagues or team members.
Two devs on my project disagreed on using REST vs GraphQL for a new endpoint. I asked each to list pros/cons, then suggested we prototype both for the top two use cases and compare latency.
What was the outcome and how did you follow up?
We picked REST after the test showed 30% lower latency. I documented the decision and checked in a week later to confirm no hard feelings.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you resolved a disagreement between colleagues or team members.
Role: new grad on small feature team; two backend devs argued API style
Actions: asked for pros/cons lists, proposed quick prototype comparison
Outcome: chose REST after latency test; documented and followed up
Quote: "I wanted to make the data decide instead of opinions."
Follow-up: Asked about long-term impact; candidate said they used same approach on next disagreement
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. The candidate owned a local disagreement by turning it into a quick data-driven test rather than picking sides. Quote shows focus on process over personal preference. Follow-up shows they repeated the pattern, indicating coachability. Biggest strength is taking initiative on interpersonal friction without escalating. Gap is narrow scope, which is expected at this level.

lowerTranscript.text: Tell me about a time you resolved a disagreement between colleagues or team members.
Two people on my team disagreed about a design. I told my manager and they handled it.
What did you do before escalating?
I just stayed out of it so I wouldn't make it worse.

raiseTranscript.text: Tell me about a time you resolved a disagreement between colleagues or team members.

Infra and app teams disagreed on rollout order for a shared service migration. I set up a joint working session, mapped dependencies on a whiteboard, and we agreed to a phased approach with clear rollback criteria.
How did you handle pushback from the louder voices?
I asked each side to state the risk they feared most, then had the other team propose mitigation. That shifted the tone to problem-solving.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you resolved a disagreement between colleagues or team members.
Role: senior engineer; cross-team migration disagreement
Actions: organized joint session, used dependency mapping and risk trade-off framing
Outcome: phased rollout plan adopted; no escalation to directors
Quote: "I made them name the actual risk instead of the preferred solution."
Follow-up: Asked about metrics; candidate tracked on-time migration and zero incidents
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. Candidate influenced two teams without authority by structuring a session around shared data rather than opinions. Quote illustrates ability to reframe debate productively. Outcome shows measurable cross-team alignment. Biggest strength is repeatable influence pattern. Gap is still mostly technical domain, as expected before manager level.

Did both sides accept your decision?
One side was unhappy but they stopped arguing after I made the call.

raiseTranscript.text: Tell me about a time you resolved a disagreement between colleagues or team members.

Two of my engineers had repeated clashes on code review standards that affected velocity. I met each 1:1 to understand their underlying concerns, then ran a team retro focused on review guidelines and had them co-own the new rubric.
What happened to their working relationship afterward?
They started pairing on reviews and velocity recovered within two sprints. I checked in monthly for three months to reinforce the new norm.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you resolved a disagreement between colleagues or team members.
Role: engineering manager; direct reports clashing on reviews
Actions: 1:1s to surface concerns, team retro, co-created rubric
Outcome: pairing started, velocity recovered; sustained check-ins
Quote: "I wanted them to own the solution so it would stick."
Follow-up: Asked about underperformance signal; candidate said one engineer had received feedback on tone
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. Candidate addressed recurring interpersonal friction by combining private listening with public ownership creation. Quote shows intent to build lasting team norms rather than temporary fixes. Sustained follow-up demonstrates investment in team health. Biggest strength is turning conflict into improved process owned by the people involved. Gap is still within one team.

raiseTranscript.text: Tell me about a time you resolved a disagreement between colleagues or team members.

Two VPs were blocking each other on a re-org decision that affected product and infrastructure roadmaps. I created a joint offsite with pre-reads on business trade-offs, facilitated a session where each presented worst-case scenarios, and we landed on a phased org model with shared OKRs.
How did this affect the broader organization?
The model was adopted company-wide within a quarter; we later used the same facilitation pattern for two other leadership conflicts.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you resolved a disagreement between colleagues or team members.
Role: director/VP; VP-level disagreement on re-org
Actions: designed offsite with scenario planning and shared OKRs
Outcome: phased model adopted org-wide; pattern reused elsewhere
Quote: "I treated it as an org capability problem, not a one-off dispute."
Follow-up: Asked about long-term leverage; candidate said two other teams adopted the framework independently
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. Candidate scaled conflict resolution into an organizational pattern rather than a personal intervention. Quote shows strategic framing around capability building. Org-wide adoption and reuse demonstrate leverage. Biggest strength is turning a single dispute into reusable process. Gap is high ambiguity tolerance required at this level, which is met here.
